post.description: Look up an Android app's store listing by package name.

country.description: Storefront country (`gl`), ISO 3166-1 alpha-2. Default US. Selects availability, prices and which reviews the store shows. Pattern: ^[A-Za-z]{2}$.

language.description: UI language (`hl`), e.g. en_US, en, de. Default en_US. Selects the language of titles, descriptions and labels; app reviews come back in the storefront language only. Pattern: ^[A-Za-z]{2}([_-][A-Za-z]{2,4})?$.

package.description: Android package name (`com.whatsapp`, `org.telegram.messenger`); the `id` of a /store/apps/details URL (a pasted details URL is accepted). Pattern: ^(https://play\.google\.com/.*[?&]id=)?[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*(\.[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)+.*$.

200.description:
One page of public user reviews of an Android app on Google Play: native review UUID, deep link, stars, text, timestamp, reviewer name, helpful count, the app version reviewed and the developer reply when there is one. Sorted by most relevant (default), newest or rating; optional star filter (`score`) and device filter (`device`: phone by default as in the store's dialog, tablet, or all). Returns an opaque `continuation` for the next page. The store does not distinguish an unknown package from a package whose reviews do not match the filter: an empty first page is reported as not_found; confirm the package with `app`.

The response contains the tool result directly.

| Documented field | Provider type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `continuation` | string | Pass as `continuation` to fetch the next page; null when the store returned no further page. |
| `count` | number | Reviews on this page. |
| `device` | string |  |
| `observed_at_ms` | number | When the program read the source, milliseconds since the Unix epoch. |
| `package` | string |  |
| `reviews` | object[] |  |
| `score` | number | Star filter applied; null when none. |
| `sort` | string |  |
| `source_url` | string | Store page the data was read from. |

value.author_bio_html:
Frank Herbert was born in Tacoma, Washington, and educated at the University of Washington, Seattle. He worked a wide variety of jobs-including TV cameraman, radio commentator, oyster diver, jungle survival instructor, lay analyst, creative writing teacher, reporter and editor of several West Coast newspapers-before becoming a full-time writer.

Scott Brick first began narrating audiobooks in 2000, and after recording almost 400 titles in five years, AudioFile magazine named Brick a Golden Voice and "one of the fastest-rising stars in the audiobook galaxy." He has read a number of titles in Frank Herbert's bestselling Dune series, and he won the 2003 Science Fiction Audie Award for Dune: The Butlerian Jihad. Brick has narrated for many popular authors, including Michael Pollan, Joseph Finder, Tom Clancy, and Ayn Rand. He has also won over 40 AudioFile Earphones Awards and the AudioFile award for Best Voice in Mystery and Suspense 2011. In 2007, Brick was named Publishers Weekly's Narrator of the Year.

Orlagh Cassidy is the winner of the 2009 Best Voice in Children & Family Listening and the 2008 and 2011 Best Voice in Mystery & Suspense. She's narrated for Jacqueline Winspear, James Patterson, Erica Spindler, Beth Harbison, and Frank Herbert, among others.

Euan Morton's narration credits include Christopher Moore's Fool and Sacre Bleu, Neil Gaiman's Stories, Eoin Colfer's Benny books, and Frank Herbert's Dune and Chapterhouse Dune. Morton's breakthrough role was appearing as Boy George in the musical Taboo, which earned him a Laurence Olivier Award nomination. He reprised the role on Broadway, earning Tony, Drama Desk, Outer Critics Circle and Drama League Award nominations, as well as the Theatre World Award (for Outstanding Broadway Debut). Morton's other stage performances include Leaves of Glass, Sondheim on Sondheim, and Cyrano De Bergerac.

Simon Vance is the critically acclaimed narrator of approximately 400 audiobooks, winner of forty-one AudioFile Earphones Awards, and a six-time Audie recipient. He was the winner of the 2012 Audie Award for Best Male Narrator, and was named the 2011 Best Voice in Biography and History and the 2010 Best Voice in fiction by AudioFile magazine. Simon was named a "Golden Voice" by Audiofile Magazine, and Booklist Magazine named him their "Voice of Choice".

Ilyana Kadushin is best known for her narration of the Twilight audiobook series, and has worked on other audiobooks, including The Memory Keeper's Daughter, Post Grad and Dune, which won an Audie Award. Her other voice work includes national commercials, animation, and popular video games such as Lord of the Rings.

reviews.text: Getting through this book was like walking through sand the way the Fremen walk through sand, which is somehow slower than the way normal people walk through sand. I think the concepts are interesting, like props to Herbert for coming up with an unique world and religion or whatever was going on there, but I'm still not sure what's going on with some stuff. Universe-specific vocab abounded, with sparse context clues. In order to understand what words or phrases meant, you had to consult the glossary. GLOSSARY! And I'm all for glossaries-- as long as they are supplemental so you can remind yourself what terms mean, not as the only way for you to learn what a Jihad is. So, yeah, it was hard to get through.

It really is not very good. I believe everyone that says it is amazing says that because the have never read it and assume it's good or they think they should say it is awesome because they are confused.  First off it is a fantasy book. There are courts, dukes, emperors and magic. Just because it takes place in the future does not it make it science fiction.  It is incredibly slow. You can add detail and make it exciting.  Dune adds detail in the excitement of a text book.
reviews.title: Meh

reviews.text: Frank Herbert creates a universe with its own religion and society, with characters that have depth (some more than others) but seem often confused. Maybe Herbert does this on purpose because he creates such a rich, detailed and complex universe that the reader (and the characters) can't absorb everything at once, so he omits things or leaves it up to the read/characters to deduce concepts and ideals. I heard and read many great things about this book, but I found it very difficult to read. It didn't become easier as I went along; just the characters and their ideals becoming more easily acclimated. With such complexity, I found that the book suffered in story; it was completely dry to say the least. The characters didn't create any emotional investment, and I honestly didn't care if they lived or died. I found the writing of Herbert to be completely atrocious. I will give Herbert credit: he did put forth effort in creativity, which I believe is the book's greatest achievement.

It was difficult to read for the first half of book (400 pages this half!), I have almost skip this book a few times. Second half was appealing thought. But in summary: I was expecting more from this novel. IMPORTANT: if you are planning to read other books from this series - do not read afterwords by author's son! He is revealing details of the following book... It is like if someone told me in advance what would be my birthday present. Like someone stealing my surprise. Why did he do this?...

although overly verbose and grandiose at times (for the entire first half of the novel, actually) frank herbert does an excellent job of building out a universe that has captivated generations of readers now. it says something that it took me over 4 years to finish (the overwhelming majority of those years spent trying to read the first half of the book), either about me or about herbert's writing style (probably both). this book is a classic and a catalyst for such creativity for good reason though.

The author's overindulgence in technobabble and gibberish adds absolutely nothing to the story. It's as if Frank Hebert is trying to convince the reader that the material is far more exotic than it actually is. The story itself isn't bad but given the buzz behind this call classic I really hoped for more
reviews.title: Overrated

reviews.text: I really enjoyed reading this book. The story was great, the action kept me on edge. I hate to admit I've actually ignored some responsibility to spend extra time reading it. I did find the language challenging. I could not find definitions for words used that fit the context in which he was using them. And many words were made up, or used incorrectly, making comprehension challenging at points. Despite THAT, it was still great. So much better than the movie, which did not do it any justice.

Fascinating concepts and world building, clunky prose and terribly stilted dialogue. FH's writing steadily improves over books 1-3 (Dune, Messiah and Children) and later books in the series are much less of a slog than the first. Absolutely worth reading, this is a phenomenal book given its historical context and is full of great ideas even if it's mechanically lacking.

7-01-2021 There are things I like and things I dislike. The story is ok, but I kind of wish it could be better in some ways. Some of the characters in the book are annoying. Most of the likable characters in this book are killed off. The story is rushed in some parts and slowed in other. The story begins leaving you hoping for something great, but keeps burning all bridges of hope, leaving me a bit disappointing. Hopefully the upcoming movie will help make the story feel a little more exciting.-- The universe the series is set is in is a bit weird, and feels more fantasy.-- Biggest problem I have with is with the author. He seems to have used a thesaurus to find the strangest words he could in place of more simpler ones. Sometimes it gets to the point where the book feels illegible. He also over indulges in the use of the word "Presently" in between dialogue/actions. The book feels unnecessary long, while the story short. Too much unnecessary exposition perhaps?

Great world. Very absorbing.  I can see why this is a sci-fi classic. However, Arrakis is definately the star of this show, and that is a shame. The characters are more like set pieces, illustrating their world's history. It is no surprise that Paul becomes less relatable as he becomes more powerful. The problem is having nobody else to cheer for. Herbert kills off all his underdogs well before the story's climax and does so much foreshadowing that by the time the big battle starts all we have left are an anointed messiah, his disciples, and an assortment of already doomed villains. If the male characters are 2 demensional, the female characters are even flatter. The big twist never comes, the forgone conclusions remain forgone, but the expert world building means this book is still worth reading.
